name: Cetylpyridinium chloride mouthwash
lead: Cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) mouthwash is an over-the-counter antiseptic rinse built around a quaternary ammonium compound that kills bacteria and disrupts the membranes of enveloped viruses.[11] Typical products contain about 0.05 percent CPC and are sold for plaque, gingivitis and bad breath.[7] The appearance payoff is a cleaner mouth: less plaque on the teeth, calmer and less inflamed gums, and fresher breath, which affect how a smile and close-up presence come across.[7][10][11]

Reviews report a small but significant added benefit on plaque and gingivitis when CPC rinses are used with toothbrushing, generally less than chlorhexidine.[11][12] Tooth staining and temporary taste changes are reported side effects.[11] During the COVID-19 pandemic, CPC rinses were also trialled for reducing SARS-CoV-2 in saliva.[2][5]

CPC is a long-standing ingredient in drugstore rinses such as Crest Pro-Health, launched in April 2005, and in lozenges, toothpastes and breath sprays; Wikipedia counted over 125 over-the-counter oral care products containing it as of September 2012.[11]

paras: CPC is used in mouthwashes, toothpastes, lozenges and throat sprays.[11] Randomised trials have compared 0.05 percent CPC rinse with 0.12 percent chlorhexidine for plaque and gingival inflammation, and with tea tree oil rinses in a short plaque regrowth model.[3][7] A 2025 double-blind trial examined CPC rinse on halitosis and tongue microbiota in people in orthodontic treatment.[10]

With chlorhexidine and zinc lactate, CPC has been found effective against halitosis, according to Wikipedia.[11] A 12-week randomized trial of a regimen combining stannous fluoride toothpaste, a rinse with 0.075 percent CPC and 0.28 percent zinc lactate, and a foaming toothbrush reported significant plaque and gingivitis reductions versus a non-antibacterial regimen from week 1 onward.[13]

Wikipedia and its cited reviews describe CPC as adding a small benefit to brushing for plaque and gingivitis.[11] A 1997 six-week double-blind study of 129 people examined effects on normal oral flora and on colonisation by non-oral species.[4] An in vitro study compared 0.05 percent chlorhexidine and 0.05 percent CPC against bacteria in biofilms, and another trial examined rinses before dental implant surgery and toothbrush disinfection.[6][8][9]

In a double-blind trial in 219 university students, alcohol-free 0.05 percent CPC and 0.12 percent chlorhexidine rinses each reduced plaque and gingivitis compared with placebo after six weeks, with no significant difference between CPC and chlorhexidine; staining scores were lower with CPC than with chlorhexidine, though not significantly so.[7] A randomized crossover trial examined CPC rinse on denture plaque and the oral microbiome.[14]

Wikipedia reports tooth staining in about 3 percent of users, and a small percentage notice temporary taste alteration that resolves a few days after stopping. Concentrated solutions irritate mucous membranes.[11] The manufacturer of Crest Pro-Health has said staining reflects the product working, because dead germs can collect on teeth, and a small back-label warning about surface staining is carried on the product.[11]

Procter and Gamble faced a class action filed in August 2009 over staining from a CPC rinse, which a US District Court dismissed in July 2010.[11] An in vitro study (2017) reported mitochondrial interference at concentrations that the authors said may be relevant to human exposure.[11] The FDA monograph concluded that 0.025 to 0.1 percent CPC is safe as an over-the-counter oral antiseptic when labeled for short-term use of up to seven days.[11]

A double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial in 118 SARS-CoV-2 positive outpatients compared 1-minute rinses with 0.07 percent CPC or coloured water; viral RNA load in saliva did not differ significantly between groups, while nucleocapsid protein from lysed viruses was higher in the CPC group at 1 hour.[2] A 2023 systematic review of randomized trials reviewed efficacy against the virus, and a lipidomics study found oral rinses disrupt the viral envelope in vivo.[5][1]

Plaque and gingivitis trials versus chlorhexidine and tea tree oil are described above.[3][7] A 1997 six-week double-blind study of 129 people examined effects of 0.05 percent CPC used twice daily on normal oral flora and on colonisation by non-oral species.[4] A 2025 double-blind trial examined CPC rinse on halitosis and tongue microbiota in people in orthodontic treatment.[10] Other trials examined rinses before dental implant surgery and toothbrush disinfection.[8][9]

timeline.event: A CPC-based rinse launches in the US market.[11]

chain: Antiseptic kills oral bacteria and reduces plaque
Less gum inflammation and less odour-producing bacterial load
Cleaner teeth, healthier-looking gums and fresher breath
angle.text: CPC rinses are used as an add-on to brushing to reduce plaque and gum inflammation and to freshen breath. Trials show a small added benefit over brushing alone; tooth staining is the main cosmetic trade-off.

card.summary: The standard drugstore antibacterial rinse; modest added plaque benefit, weaker than chlorhexidine, with some staining.
card.note: Tooth staining in a small share of users; temporary taste changes reported.

quick.overview:
CPC mouthwash is the common over-the-counter antibacterial rinse, usually at about 0.05 percent. Reviews describe a small added benefit over brushing alone for plaque and gum inflammation.

It also drew research interest during COVID-19 because it breaks down the lipid coat of some viruses.
quick.mechanism: CPC is a positively charged quaternary ammonium compound that binds to and disrupts bacterial and viral membranes.
quick.risks: Tooth staining is reported in roughly 3 percent of users and taste alteration is usually temporary. The US FDA monograph covers short-term OTC use at 0.025 to 0.1 percent.
